title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
pub: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia, File No. SC-2023-005609 (Tribunal Member Christopher C. Rivers)
author: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia

dom.t: Chatbot liability: Correct links do not cure misinformation

st.t: Chatbot liability: Correct links do not cure misinformation
st.an: The decision directly supports the cluster: it applies negligent-misrepresentation law to chatbot advice, holds Air Canada responsible regardless of delivery format, finds reliance reasonable despite a link to conflicting policy information, and bases relief on proven reliance, loss and failed defences. It also confirms that the chatbot’s underlying technology was not established.
qs: It should be obvious to Air Canada that it is responsible for all the information on its website.
It also does not explain why customers should have to double-check information found in one part of its website on another part of its website.

mo.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control

kp.k: Chatbot advice contradicted the airline’s bereavement policy
kp.d: The dispute arose from November 2022 bookings following the death of Mr. Moffatt’s grandmother. A screenshot showed the chatbot advising that passengers could seek a reduced bereavement rate within 90 days after ticket issuance, including after travel. A linked Air Canada webpage instead excluded requests after travel had been completed. Air Canada later acknowledged misleading wording. The tribunal expressly noted that Air Canada supplied no information about the chatbot’s nature; the decision does not identify its underlying technology.
qs: If you need to travel immediately or have already travelled and would like to submit your ticket for a reduced bereavement rate, kindly do so within 90 days of the date your ticket was issued by completing our Ticket Refund Application form.
The webpage says, in part, the bereavement policy does not apply to requests for bereavement consideration after travel has been completed.

While Air Canada did not provide any information about the nature of its chatbot, generally speaking, a chatbot is an automated system that provides information to a person using a website in response to that person’s prompts and input.

kp.k: Ordinary negligent misrepresentation principles governed chatbot advice
kp.d: The tribunal characterised Mr. Moffatt’s reliance claim as negligent misrepresentation, although the applicant did not use that terminology. It applied requirements of duty, misleading representation, negligence, reasonable reliance and resulting damages. The commercial service-provider–consumer relationship established a duty of care, and Air Canada failed to take reasonable care to ensure accurate chatbot information. This was a finding in a consumer dispute, not a prediction about legal-service automation.
qs: To prove the tort of negligent misrepresentation, Mr. Moffatt must show that Air Canada owed them a duty of care, its representation was untrue, inaccurate, or misleading, Air Canada made the representation negligently, Mr. Moffatt reasonably relied on it, and Mr. Moffatt’s reliance resulted in damages.
Here, given their commercial relationship as a service provider and consumer, I find Air Canada owed Mr. Moffatt a duty of care.
I find Air Canada did not take reasonable care to ensure its chatbot was accurate.

kp.k: Air Canada remained responsible for its chatbot’s information
kp.d: Air Canada argued that it could not be liable for information supplied by its agents, servants or representatives, including a chatbot. The tribunal rejected that unexplained position, characterising it as effectively treating the chatbot as a separate legal entity. Its reasoning treated interactive chatbot information as part of the company’s website, with no relevant distinction from information on static pages.
qs: Air Canada argues it cannot be held liable for information provided by one of its agents, servants, or representatives – including a chatbot.
In effect, Air Canada suggests the chatbot is a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions.
While a chatbot has an interactive component, it is still just a part of Air Canada’s website.
It makes no difference whether the information comes from a static page or a chatbot.

kp.k: Conflicting website information did not defeat reasonable reliance
kp.d: The tribunal accepted that Mr. Moffatt reasonably relied on the chatbot and would not have flown last-minute knowing the full fare would apply. Air Canada did not explain why its linked policy webpage was more trustworthy or why customers should cross-check one part of its website against another. The applicant’s investigation of bereavement options and diligent refund requests supported the finding of reliance.
qs: It also does not explain why customers should have to double-check information found in one part of its website on another part of its website.
Mr. Moffatt says, and I accept, that they relied upon the chatbot to provide accurate information. I find that was reasonable in the circumstances.
Mr. Moffatt says, and I accept, that they would not have flown last-minute if they knew they would have to pay the full fare.

kp.k: Missing evidence undermined contractual and damages defences
kp.d: The tribunal rejected Air Canada’s contractual defence because it supplied assertions about its Domestic Tariff rather than the relevant contractual text; it did not decide that the alleged terms were substantively invalid. Separately, Air Canada provided no contrary fare evidence despite being best positioned to do so. The tribunal drew an adverse inference and accepted $380 as the bereavement fare’s market value before additional charges and taxes.
qs: I find that if Air Canada wanted to a raise a contractual defense, it needed to provide the relevant portions of the contract. It did not, so it has not proven a contractual defence.
An adverse inference is where an adjudicator assumes a party has failed to provide relevant evidence because the missing evidence would not support their case.
Here, I find that if Air Canada had evidence of a different bereavement fare, it would have provided it.
Since Mr. Moffatt says they were told the fare was $380, I find that does not include the additional costs of taxes, security charges, or airport improvement fees that they also had to pay.

kp.k: Misrepresentation produced damages, interest and fee reimbursement
kp.d: The tribunal mostly allowed the claim, awarding $650.88 in damages rather than the $880 requested. Its damages calculation stated that the two flights should have cost $979.48 rather than $1,630.36. It denied a $200 coupon set-off because acceptance was not established. The final payment order totalled $812.02: damages, $36.14 in pre-judgment interest and $125 in CRT fees, with post-judgment interest also applicable. These are the decision’s stated calculations and award.
qs: Mr. Moffatt is entitled to be put in the position they would have been in if the misrepresentation had not been made.
In total, then, I find Mr. Moffatt should have paid $979.48 for their two flights. Since they paid $1,630.36, I find they are entitled to damages of $650.88.
However, Mr. Moffatt says they did not accept the offered coupon, and Air Canada has provided no evidence to show otherwise. So, I find Air Canada is not entitled to any set-off.
Within 14 days of the date of this order, I order Air Canada to pay Mr. Moffatt a total of $812.02, broken down as follows:

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tribunal Member Christopher C. Rivers finds that Air Canada was responsible for misleading information supplied by its website chatbot and liable for negligent misrepresentation when a customer reasonably relied on it.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain adjudicative finding about automated airline customer service, not a prediction about legal services. Rivers rejects Air Canada's attempt to disclaim responsibility for chatbot information: an interactive chatbot remains part of the company's website. He also finds that linking to a separate, accurate policy page did not establish that customers should double-check the chatbot's information. The decision does not identify the chatbot's technology as generative AI or establish that its misleading output was a generative-model hallucination.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The findings rest on documentary evidence of contradictory website information, Air Canada's acknowledgment of misleading wording, accepted evidence of customer reliance, and negligent-misrepresentation doctrine.
pts.d: Rivers considers a screenshot in which the chatbot said passengers could request a reduced bereavement rate within 90 days, a separate policy page excluding requests after completed travel, booking and refund correspondence, and a company representative's acknowledgment of the error. He accepts Moffatt's evidence that they relied on the chatbot and would not have flown last-minute at full fare. The legal test is supported by Queen v. Cognos Inc.; the damages principle is supported by Ban v. Keleher. These are findings in one dispute on a balance of probabilities, not model benchmarks or evidence of chatbot error rates. Air Canada supplied no technical account of the chatbot and failed to provide the tariff provisions needed to establish its asserted contractual defence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2024 decision addresses reliance on chatbot information in November 2022; liability is tied to the established elements of negligent misrepresentation, not a forecast or an unconditional rule covering every chatbot error.
pts.d: Moffatt booked flights on November 11 and 16, 2022, and first applied for the bereavement fare on November 17, within the chatbot's stated 90-day period. Correspondence continued into 2023. Rivers finds a duty of care arising from the service-provider/consumer relationship, negligent misleading information, reasonable reliance in the circumstances, and resulting loss. Air Canada's contractual defence was unproven because it did not submit the relevant contract provisions; the decision does not determine the effectiveness of every possible contractual limitation. The payment order required compliance within 14 days.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected parties are an airline deploying automated customer support and a consumer who incurred costs after relying on that support.
pts.d: Air Canada bears responsibility for taking reasonable care over its website representations, including chatbot responses. Moffatt's reliance was held reasonable despite the availability of a contradictory linked page, and they received an award of $650.88 in damages, $36.14 in pre-judgment interest, and $125 in tribunal fees, totaling $812.02. The source makes no claim about lawyer displacement, legal-market restructuring, or AI-driven access to justice; the parties' self-representation and employee representation are procedural facts rather than demonstrated effects of AI.
